blocks.heading: Using statements and ratios together
blocks.text: An Income Statement reports income, expenses and resulting profit or loss for a period. A Statement of Financial Position reports assets, liabilities and equity at a date. Ratios relate selected figures to answer a specific question. Profitability includes gross and net profit margins and return on capital employed. Liquidity concerns ability to meet short-term debts and is indicated by current and quick ratios. Inventory turnover concerns how quickly stock is used or sold and is an efficiency measure in Annexe A, even though it also influences liquidity. The solvency ratio here is total assets divided by total liabilities, expressed x:1. Do not replace it with a different textbook’s debt percentage. Compare ratios with an earlier period, similar business or relevant conditions. A high current ratio can reflect slow inventory, and strong reported profit does not establish prompt cash receipts. Use year-end balances where appropriate unless average figures are specified. Give ratio answers to two decimal places and distinguish percentages, x:1, days and times per annum.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri Traders: annual turnover N$240,000, cost of sales N$144,000, other expenses N$72,000, credit sales N$219,000 and credit purchases N$146,000. At year end: non-current assets N$90,000; inventory N$30,000; debtors N$18,000; cash N$12,000; current liabilities N$30,000 (including creditors N$20,000); non-current liabilities N$40,000; owner’s equity N$80,000. Opening inventory was N$18,000. Use the opening and closing inventory average for inventory turnover. No other income or expense is assumed in this simple example. Neri’s gross margin is 40.00%, net margin 10.00%, ROCE 20.00%, current ratio 2.00:1 and quick ratio 1.00:1. Its solvency ratio is 2.14:1 rounded. Inventory turnover is 6.00 times per annum using the specified average. These describe different aspects: the gap between the current and quick ratios highlights inventory’s importance, while profit margins do not tell us when debtors pay.

blocks.heading: Income Statement
blocks.text: An Income Statement reports income and expenses and the resulting profit or loss over a period. Read the heading to identify the period. Sales less cost of sales gives gross profit; deduct the other relevant expenses and add any other specified income to find net profit. It measures performance, not the total assets owned at one date. A profitable statement can contain credit sales not yet collected.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri reports turnover N$240,000, cost of sales N$144,000 and other expenses N$72,000. The statement shows gross profit N$96,000 and net profit N$24,000 for the year. It does not state that all sales have been collected or that those profits remain in cash.

blocks.heading: Statement of Financial Position
blocks.text: A Statement of Financial Position reports assets, liabilities and equity at a particular date. It separates current and non-current categories so users can examine resources and obligations. Assets equal equity plus liabilities when the statement is complete and consistently prepared. It describes recorded position rather than revenue earned over a period. Book values do not guarantee sale proceeds and year-end balances may not describe every day of the year.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Neri has non-current assets N$90,000, current assets N$60,000, current liabilities N$30,000, non-current liabilities N$40,000 and equity N$80,000. Assets total N$150,000. Liabilities plus equity also total N$150,000. The equality shows how the resources are financed; it does not establish their cash realisation or profitability.

blocks.heading: Return on capital employed
blocks.text: ROCE = net profit / capital employed × 100. Capital employed is owner’s capital plus long-term liabilities using year-end figures here. ROCE relates annual profit to the long-term finance invested, so it measures return rather than short-term bill-paying ability. Compare like periods and accounting bases; a higher percentage can reflect improved profit or a reduced denominator and needs explanation.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Neri has net profit N$24,000, owner’s equity N$80,000 and long-term liabilities N$40,000. Capital employed is N$120,000. ROCE = 24,000 / 120,000 × 100, giving 20.00%. The business earns N$20 annual net profit per N$100 capital employed under these figures.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Re-read after expressing percentage conversions explicitly and qualifying average-cost changes with capacity and coordination conditions; the unchanged numerical examples and comparisons still hold.

blocks.heading: Gross profit margin
blocks.text: Gross profit margin = gross profit / turnover × 100. It shows the percentage of sales revenue left after cost of sales, before other expenses. A higher margin might arise from higher selling prices, a different product mix or lower purchase costs. It does not by itself show a higher cash balance or net profit; other expenses and sales volume matter.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Neri has gross profit N$96,000 and turnover N$240,000. Gross margin = 96,000 / 240,000 × 100, giving 40.00%. N$40 of each N$100 sales remains to meet other expenses and provide net profit.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Re-read after expressing percentage conversions explicitly and qualifying average-cost changes with capacity and coordination conditions; the unchanged numerical examples and comparisons still hold.

blocks.heading: Net profit margin
blocks.text: Net profit margin = net profit / turnover × 100. It shows the percentage of sales left as net profit after the included costs and expenses. Compare it with gross margin to examine how other expenses affect performance. A high percentage on low sales can still produce a smaller absolute profit than a lower percentage on very high sales. It is not a cash-flow measure.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Neri has net profit N$24,000 and turnover N$240,000. Net margin = 24,000 / 240,000 × 100, giving 10.00%. N$10 of each N$100 sales remains as net profit.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Re-read after expressing percentage conversions explicitly and qualifying average-cost changes with capacity and coordination conditions; the unchanged numerical examples and comparisons still hold.

blocks.heading: Current ratio
blocks.text: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities, expressed x:1. It compares short-term resources with short-term obligations, not profit with sales. A high figure may provide a cushion, but inventory can be slow-moving and debtors may pay late. A very high figure can also indicate funds tied up unproductively. A suitable level depends on the business and cash cycle rather than one universal ideal.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Neri has current assets N$60,000 and current liabilities N$30,000. Current ratio = 60,000 / 30,000 = 2.00:1. N$2 current assets back each N$1 current liabilities, but some resources must be converted into cash.

blocks.heading: Quick or liquid ratio
blocks.text: Quick ratio = (current assets − inventory) / current liabilities, expressed x:1. It removes inventory to examine coverage without depending on its sale. Debtors included in the remaining assets still need to pay, so a quick ratio is not a cash ratio and cannot guarantee immediate settlement. Compare with the current ratio to see how strongly coverage depends on stock.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Neri has current assets N$60,000, inventory N$30,000 and current liabilities N$30,000. Quick ratio = (60,000 − 30,000) / 30,000 = 1.00:1. N$1 non-inventory current assets backs each N$1 current liabilities.

blocks.heading: Rate of inventory turnover
blocks.text: Rate of inventory turnover = cost of sales / average inventory, expressed times per annum for annual figures. Use the average inventory specified; if opening and closing balances are given for that purpose, add them and divide by two. It indicates how often the average inventory is sold or used over the year. Faster turnover can release cash and reduce storage, but may mean inadequate stock if it causes shortages. Compare similar products: fresh food and durable furniture have different expected cycles.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Neri has cost of sales N$144,000 and opening and closing inventory N$18,000 and N$30,000. Use their average. Average inventory = (18,000 + 30,000) / 2 = N$24,000. Inventory turnover = 144,000 / 24,000 = 6.00 times per annum.

blocks.heading: Solvency ratio
blocks.text: Solvency ratio in this syllabus = total assets / total liabilities, expressed x:1. Include current and non-current liabilities in the denominator. It indicates recorded asset coverage of total obligations. A value above 1 indicates recorded assets exceed liabilities, but realisable values can differ and long-lived assets may not pay debts due today. It therefore differs from liquidity and from profit margin. Do not substitute a debt-to-equity or debt-percentage formula.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Neri has total assets N$150,000 and total liabilities N$70,000. Solvency ratio = 150,000 / 70,000, rounded to 2.14:1. Recorded assets are about N$2.14 per N$1 total liabilities, not N$2.14 cash per debt dollar.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Financial evidence and judgement
blocks.text:
Fictional Neri Traders: annual turnover N$240,000, cost of sales N$144,000, other expenses N$72,000, credit sales N$219,000 and credit purchases N$146,000. At year end: non-current assets N$90,000; inventory N$30,000; debtors N$18,000; cash N$12,000; current liabilities N$30,000 (including creditors N$20,000); non-current liabilities N$40,000; owner’s equity N$80,000. Opening inventory was N$18,000. Use the opening and closing inventory average for inventory turnover. No other income or expense is assumed in this simple example. A supplier is considering another short credit sale to Neri and wants evidence of prompt payment. A shareholder is assessing returns. Supplier payment terms for existing creditors are forty-five days.

a Analyse Neri’s profitability and liquidity using gross margin, net margin and quick ratio, and distinguish these measures from solvency. [8]
b Evaluate whether the supplied financial evidence is enough for a supplier to extend further forty-five-day credit. [12]

a Gross profit = 240,000 − 144,000 = N$96,000, giving gross margin 40.00%. Net profit is N$24,000, giving net margin 10.00%. The thirty-percentage-point difference is the burden of other included expenses relative to turnover. Quick ratio is 1.00:1, showing non-inventory current assets equal current liabilities, but payment timing still matters. Solvency is total assets N$150,000 divided by total liabilities N$70,000, rounded to 2.14:1; this is total asset cover rather than a measure of cash due soon. No earlier-period data establishes whether performance improved. b The statements provide useful evidence: a profit, positive working capital and non-inventory asset coverage. Collection period is 30.00 days and creditor period 50.00 days under the annual estimates. Against this, the creditor estimate already exceeds forty-five-day terms and year-end ratios can conceal near-term cash gaps or overdue individual accounts. Inventory forms half the current assets and some assets are long-lived. The supplier needs current cash-flow timing and payment history before choosing a credit limit; profitable trading is insufficient. Extend limited credit only if the updated evidence supports the deadline and monitor payment. Otherwise request safer terms or postpone rather than inferring certainty from ratios.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Financial evidence and judgement
blocks.text:
Fictional Neri Traders: annual turnover N$240,000, cost of sales N$144,000, other expenses N$72,000, credit sales N$219,000 and credit purchases N$146,000. At year end: non-current assets N$90,000; inventory N$30,000; debtors N$18,000; cash N$12,000; current liabilities N$30,000 (including creditors N$20,000); non-current liabilities N$40,000; owner’s equity N$80,000. Opening inventory was N$18,000. Use the opening and closing inventory average for inventory turnover. No other income or expense is assumed in this simple example. A supplier is considering another short credit sale to Neri and wants evidence of prompt payment. A shareholder is assessing returns. Supplier payment terms for existing creditors are forty-five days.

a(i) Define unit cost. [2]
a(ii) State two users of financial statements. [2]
b State one fixed and one variable cost for a furniture workshop. [2]
c Analyse what Neri’s current and quick ratios reveal about its short-term position; show the ratios. [6]
d Evaluate whether the supplier should rely on Neri’s net profit figure alone when deciding to offer further credit. [8]

a(i) Total production cost divided by total output, expressed per item. a(ii) Shareholders and lenders. b Fixed workshop rent and variable timber used per item. c Current assets = 30,000 + 18,000 + 12,000 = N$60,000. Current ratio = 60,000 / 30,000, expressed as 2.00:1. Quick ratio = (60,000 − 30,000) / 30,000, expressed as 1.00:1. Excluding inventory halves coverage, so stock conversion matters. Debtors are still not cash; ratios alone do not establish payment on a particular date. d Net profit N$24,000 shows a surplus over the year but not receipts available on the supplier’s due date. The supplier should examine cash forecasts, debtor collection, existing payments and credit history. The fifty-day creditor estimate exceeds stated forty-five-day terms, so further credit needs particular care. Do not rely on profit alone; grant appropriate credit only if updated evidence supports on-time payment, otherwise limit or postpone it.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why fictional Ava Traders can be profitable and show positive solvency cover while struggling to pay next week’s supplier. It reports a profit, most assets are long-lived equipment, inventory is slow-moving and customers have not paid.

Profitability concerns the surplus or return earned over a period. Solvency here compares total recorded assets with total liabilities. Liquidity concerns meeting short-term debts as they fall due. Equipment and slow-moving stock may provide recorded asset cover without becoming cash before next week, while unpaid sales can contribute to profit before collection. The three measures therefore cannot be substituted for one another.
